Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Quick technical demo showing adapter approach for switching endpoints from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Walkthrough of API parity mapping, console features (rollouts, metrics), and Optimize recommendations (batching, quantization). Discussed data residency, KMS, SOC 2 questions and pilot next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right, thanks everyone for joining, we wanted to run through a short technical preview — adapter swap approach for Summit AI. I'm Jordan from Redwood, with Priya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Marcus Chen: Good, thanks. Quick heads up, we only have about an hour, we wanna focus on the delta - what's different if we switch from our OpenAI/Together endpoints.
[00:20] Priya Nair: Great, we'll keep it tight. I'll demo the console and then dig into the parity mapping and Optimize suggestions. There might be a couple typos in the transcribe, sorry in advance, live captions can be a little rough.
[00:30] Aisha Rahman: No worries. Also Farah will pepper in security Qs at the end.
[00:35] Farah Patel: Yup.
[01:05] Priya Nair: Ok starting with the API - Redwood exposes a single /v1/generate and /v1/chat style surface, designed to be drop-in. For example your Together J1 calls — you can keep same prompt structure, but we recommend a small adapter: map function-calling arguments and streaming tokens. We have an example repo, basically two files: adapter.ts and token-normalize.py. I'll paste link after.
[01:40] Diego Morales: Question — Together uses a slightly different tokenization and role schema, will that blow up our prompt scoring?
[01:49] Priya Nair: Good point. Tokenization differences matter mostly for cost estimates and kv cache alignment. Redwood's tokenizer is compatible with most open models, but for parity you can normalise tokens in the adapter (we show a snippet that does whitespace and role mapping). In practice we've seen < 3% diff on token counts for J1-like models after normalisation.
[02:15] Marcus Chen: And function calling? We use it heavily in our orchestration layer.
[02:22] Priya Nair: We support function/tool calling, it's wire-compatible but namespacing is slightly different — you can either map names in adapter or use Redwood's function_aliases feature in the request header. Example: header X-Function-Alias: external_name->internal_name. There was a small typo in the doc earlier where it said X-FuncAlias but it's X-Function-Alias, sorry.
[03:00] Jordan Lee: Now switching to console - quick tour. I'll share my screen... (screen share noise)
[03:20] Speaker 1: [screen share starts] Console shows per-route latency, cost/token, and token histogram. Under Rollouts you can configure canary percent and auto-fallback to a cheaper quantised model if latency breaches SLO.
[03:45] Aisha Rahman: Can we see request traces down to prompt level?
[03:52] Priya Nair: Yes, redwood.trace captures request->model->latency and you can filter by token buckets. We store anonymized prompt fingerprints by default, full prompts retained only if you opt in under enterprise retention. That was a mouthful — basically, you control retention.
[04:20] Farah Patel: About KMS and encryption at rest? We need customer-managed keys.
[04:28] Jordan Lee: Absolutely, Private deployments support KMS/HSM integrations; for Hosted we offer HSM-backed encryption and bring-your-own-key for Dedicated. We'll share the security pack with exact diagrams.
[04:45] Marcus Chen: On performance — we run low-latency chat on 2k context and some reranking at 8k. How does Redwood handle kv cache and larger contexts?
[04:56] Priya Nair: Runtime handles KV cache with sharded KV storage and eviction policies. For 8k sequences we recommend dedicated capacity with mixed precision/quantized models — Redwood Optimize will recommend the right quantization profile based on your seq-length distribution. We'll likely suggest a 4-bit Q4 profile for reranking to cut cost ~2.5x while keeping quality.
[05:20] Diego Morales: That sounds promising. For dedicated — what's the autoscale window?
[05:25] Jordan Lee: You can configure autoscale based on P99 latency and queue depth; default is 2 minute smoothing and a 5-minute cool-down, but all tunable.
[06:05] Priya Nair: Demo piece — here's a quick parity mapping table. I'm reading: OpenAI GPT-4o equivalent maps to redwood/gptx-large-v1 for throughput parity, Anthropic Claude-2 ~ redwood/claude-compat-v1, Together-J1 -> redwood/together-compat-v1. These are guidance mappings; we run your pilot to pick the best fit. (Note: mapping names sometimes change in console - check model catalog for latest).
[06:40] Marcus Chen: Are those models we host or are they wrappers? We don't want vendor lock-in if Redwood's model names change.
[06:47] Priya Nair: They are variants hosted/managed by Redwood; you can pin model hashes in both Hosted and Dedicated. The console records the exact model artifact id. If you need full portability we also support export manifests for on-prem/private deployments.
[07:10] Farah Patel: Audit logs — are all token-level requests logged? We need full traceability for SOC 2.
[07:16] Jordan Lee: Audit logs include metadata and request fingerprints; full prompt logging is opt-in and we can route prompt storage to your S3 with encryption. SOC 2 docs in the security pack show retention controls and access audit.
[07:40] [08:00] Priya Nair: Now Optimize — this is where we automatically suggest batching and caching. Example: your reranking workload had many short queries that benefit from 16ms batching with 4-8 concurrency; Optimize suggested prefix caching for common prompts which cut token costs 18%. We can run Optimize in dry-run so you can see simulated cost savings.
[08:30] Aisha Rahman: Does Optimize change model outputs? Concerned about quality regressions from quantization.
[08:38] Priya Nair: We guard with evaluations. Optimize will generate a recommended quant profile and then run your provided eval prompts through baseline and candidate models and produce delta metrics (KL, EM, rouge-ish). You can set thresholds for auto-apply. We also expose human review flows.
[09:10] Diego Morales: Ok, what about streaming compatibility — we rely on SSE streaming and partial deltas.
[09:18] Priya Nair: Redwood supports streaming SSE and websocket. One caveat — because of continuous batching sometimes small tail tokens can be buffered for up to 50-100ms; you can set a low-latency policy to prioritize immediate flush at cost of throughput. That option is per-route in console.
[10:00] Marcus Chen: Great. Let's go deeper — can you show an adapter snippet?
[10:15] Priya Nair: Sure. (reads) sample pseudo:

function transformRequest(externalReq) {
  // role map: user->usr, assistant->sys (your schema)
  externalReq.role = mapRoles(externalReq.role);
  // token normalise: collapse whitespace, unicode norm
  externalReq.prompt = normalizeTokens(externalReq.prompt);
  // function alias header
  headers['X-Function-Alias'] = 'external->internal';
  return externalReq;
}

[10:45] Aisha Rahman: So that's run in your sidecar? We don't want to send plain prompts through a third party transform.
[10:55] Jordan Lee: The adapter can run on your side — we recommend putting it in your API gateway or lambda. For Hosted customers we provide a thin adapter you can run in your VPC (no prompt leaves your network until forwarded).
[11:20] Farah Patel: That helps. For VPC peering — we're Azure-only, any gotchas?
[11:27] Priya Nair: Azure works. Dedicated + Private both support Azure VNet peering; sometimes firewall NAT rules block health-checks, we provide a checklist. Diego we can sync after for network details.
[11:45] Diego Morales: Will do.
[12:05] [12:30] Marcus Chen: Benchmarks — can we get a run of our real prompts on Redwood infra?
[12:38] Jordan Lee: Yes, pilot plan we discussed: 2-week pilot, we run 24-48h benchmark with your prompts against candidate models and config (quant profiles, batching). We'll share a spreadsheet with per-prompt latency/cost and quality deltas.
[13:10] Priya Nair: We'll also show simulated monthly cost at your QPS. You'll get a per-token and per-embedding breakdown as part of the pilot report.
[13:40] Aisha Rahman: About embeddings — we use embedding vectors heavily for retrieval. Are embeddings the same model families?
[13:48] Priya Nair: We have dedicated embedding models and also multi-task models. For migration, we map OpenAI embeddings to redwood/embed-1 and recommend reindexing windows. If you need feature parity (dot product, cosine) we expose normalization helpers in SDK.
[14:20] Farah Patel: For compliance we have data residency needs EU-only.
[14:25] Jordan Lee: Private deployment or region-pinned Dedicated are options. For hosted we have EU region with data residency controls. We'll note this as a requirement in the SOW.
[14:50] [15:10] Priya Nair: Quick note on costs — migration often reduces unit cost by 20-60% depending on quantization and batching. For reranking we usually see the larger wins. But customers trade-off if they need strict output parity.
[15:40] Marcus Chen: Are there customer references that did a similar switch?
[15:47] Jordan Lee: Yes, we've worked with Nova Labs and Quanta Systems on adapter swap pilots — I'll include redacted case notes.
[16:05] Diego Morales: Ok let's talk failure modes — what happens if the Redwood model deviates on hallucinations?
[16:12] Priya Nair: We recommend an A/B rollout and red-team eval. You can set auto-fallback to your previous provider via the routing policy in the console while you monitor quality. Also an option: run shadowing where you mirror requests to Redwood but don't serve responses to users, compare deltas.
[16:45] Marcus Chen: Shadowing might be the safest path.
[16:48] Priya Nair: Agreed.
[17:10] [17:40] Farah Patel: Security: SSO, SAML, RBAC mapping — what is supported?
[17:46] Jordan Lee: SSO via SAML and OIDC supported, granular RBAC, role sync with SCIM. For audit we can stream logs to your SIEM.
[18:10] Aisha Rahman: Any limitations around fine-tuning or adapters? We do some light fine-tune with proprietary instruction sets.
[18:18] Priya Nair: Hosted doesn't let you bring custom GPU fine-tune artifacts yet, but Dedicated and Private support customer artifacts and fine-tuning workflows. For quick signal you can use instruction tuning via prompt templates and few-shot. We'll help plan the approach.
[19:00] Marcus Chen: What's the SLA for Dedicated? We need 99.9 for some routes.
[19:06] Jordan Lee: We offer SLA up to 99.95 for Dedicated plans; specifics will be in the contract.
[19:40] Diego Morales: For pilot budgeting — what's rough cost of running the benchmark?
[19:45] Jordan Lee: Pilot benchmarking typically billed as a small fixed fee to cover reserved capacity plus usage; we'll include exact numbers in the SOW.
[20:12] [20:40] Priya Nair: Now a console quick demo of Optimize recommendations (screen again) — here's a sample suggestion: for your chat endpoint, set batch window 12ms, max tokens per batch 512, enable prefix KV caching for top-20 recurring prompts. The console shows expected cost delta and an eval scoring showing delta <0.8% on F1 for our sample set.
[21:15] Aisha Rahman: Does that integrate with our CI so we can run evals on new prompt sets?
[21:22] Priya Nair: Yes, we expose an eval API so you can push your prompt suite and we will run daily or on-demand. Results go to the console and can be exported.
[21:50] Marcus Chen: Couple of nitpicks — our infra uses mutual TLS between services, will that be a problem with Redwood SDKs?
[21:58] Jordan Lee: Mutual TLS is supported for Dedicated and Private. For Hosted we usually use standard TLS with token-based auth; if mTLS is a hard requirement we can discuss a Private deployment.
[22:30] Farah Patel: Ok security Qs done for now, thanks.
[22:45] Priya Nair: Nice — moving to a short Q&A, then we'll recap next steps.
